sections.overview: Aurelia aurita is a translucent scyphozoan, or true jellyfish, whose familiar saucer-shaped medusa is only one part of its life cycle. Once treated as cosmopolitan, the species was later separated from many similar Aurelia; A. aurita is now reported mainly from the northeastern Atlantic, with introduced populations in northeastern US and Argentina, though natural arrival in the US remains possible.
sections.identification: A typical adult bell is about 25–40 cm across. Four horseshoe-shaped gonads show through it, above four oral arms and fine marginal tentacles; the clear body may have a faint blue or pink tint. The consulted species references do not provide a reliable adult body mass for identification; no weight is estimated here.
sections.habitat: The medusa lives in pelagic water; its polyp is benthic and attaches to a hard surface, often under shelter in shallow brackish sites.
sections.diet: Tentacles and bell mucus intercept zooplankton, including copepods and small larvae. Cnidocytes are stinging cells containing nematocysts, tiny capsules that fire venomous harpoons when prey touches a tentacle. The same contact-triggered discharge can stun predators, so these cells serve defense as well as feeding. Cilia carry captured food along the oral arms to the mouth and gastrovascular cavity for digestion.
sections.behavior: Bell pulses propel the medusa briefly, while currents carry it farther. Medusae may gather to breed; attached polyps bud asexually.
sections.reproduction: Adults have separate sexes; males release sperm, and fertilized eggs develop in brood pockets on female oral arms. The ciliated planula swims briefly before settling and becoming a small attached polyp, or scyphistoma. The polyp may bud, then strobilate: constrictions segment it and release disc-shaped ephyrae. Ephyrae develop into adult medusae. Seasonal temperature affects strobilation timing.
sections.ecology: Podocysts, protective resting cysts produced by polyps, help them endure food shortages and resist nudibranch predation during the benthic stage.
sections.conservation: Periodic local blooms can strand jellies on beaches or clog coastal seawater intakes, creating a local infrastructure problem rather than evidence of a global population decline.

sources.title: Jellyfish Tentacles Close Up, Smithsonian Ocean
